blocks.en: 1. A Witness That Speaks in Stone
blocks.es_reference: 1. Un Testigo que Habla en Piedra

blocks.en: A third witness now rises, and it is unlike the first two. The witness of the canon spoke in the church's recognition of its books; the witness of the text spoke in ink and parchment. This third witness speaks in stone. It is the evidence of archaeology — the buried cities, the clay tablets, the carved inscriptions, the broken pottery and toppled walls that the spade lifts out of the ground. Its testimony is real and valuable, but it is easily misunderstood, and misunderstanding it has done great harm on both sides. So before we look at any single discovery, we must learn how this witness actually testifies — what archaeology can do, what it cannot, and how an honest believer should weigh it. This unit sets the rules; the next will walk among the actual finds. And the rule that governs everything here can be stated in three words: correlation, not proof. Archaeology can show, again and again, that the world of the Bible was a real world — real kings, real cities, real customs in real places. That is correlation, and it is a genuine and powerful thing. But it is not the same as proof, and the believer who confuses the two, in either direction, will stumble. Let us learn to hear this witness rightly.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora se levanta un tercer testigo, y es distinto de los dos primeros. El testigo del canon habló en el reconocimiento que la iglesia hizo de sus libros; el testigo del texto habló en tinta y pergamino. Este tercer testigo habla en piedra. Es la evidencia de la arqueología — las ciudades sepultadas, las tablillas de barro, las inscripciones talladas, la cerámica rota y los muros derribados que la pala levanta de la tierra. Su testimonio es real y valioso, pero se malentiende con facilidad, y malentenderlo ha hecho gran daño en ambos lados. Así que antes de mirar un solo descubrimiento, debemos aprender cómo testifica en verdad este testigo — qué puede hacer la arqueología, qué no puede, y cómo un creyente honesto debe pesarla. Esta unidad fija las reglas; la próxima caminará entre los hallazgos reales. Y la regla que gobierna todo aquí puede decirse en tres palabras: correlación, no prueba. La arqueología puede mostrar, una y otra vez, que el mundo de la Biblia era un mundo real — reyes reales, ciudades reales, costumbres reales en lugares reales. Eso es correlación, y es algo genuino y poderoso. Pero no es lo mismo que prueba, y el creyente que confunde las dos, en cualquier dirección, tropezará. Aprendamos a oír a este testigo correctamente.

blocks.en: 2. What Archaeology Is, and Is Not
blocks.es_reference: 2. Qué Es la Arqueología, y Qué No Es

blocks.en: First, what is archaeology, and what is it not? Archaeology is the recovery and interpretation of the material remains of the past — the physical things that people long dead left behind. It is, by its nature, a science of fragments. Consider how little survives and how little is recovered. Only a small fraction of the ancient sites that once existed have ever been located; of those, only a fraction have been excavated; of any site that is dug, only a portion is ever opened; and of what is opened, most of what was once there has perished — the wood, the cloth, the leather, the papyrus, the flesh, all gone, leaving mostly stone and baked clay. Written inscriptions, which tell us the most, are the rarest survivals of all. And every object that is found must still be interpreted — dated, identified, fitted into a story — and interpretation can be revised. So archaeology is not a machine that you feed a Bible verse into and receive a verdict of "true" or "false." It is a patient, partial, human reading of the scattered leftovers of the past. Understanding that limitation is the beginning of using this witness honestly, for it explains at once why archaeology so rarely proves, and why its silence proves even less.
blocks.es_reference: Primero, ¿qué es la arqueología, y qué no es? La arqueología es la recuperación e interpretación de los restos materiales del pasado — las cosas físicas que dejaron atrás personas muertas hace mucho. Es, por su naturaleza, una ciencia de fragmentos. Considera cuán poco sobrevive y cuán poco se recupera. Solo una pequeña fracción de los sitios antiguos que alguna vez existieron han sido localizados; de esos, solo una fracción han sido excavados; de cualquier sitio que se excava, solo una porción se abre jamás; y de lo que se abre, la mayor parte de lo que allí hubo ha perecido — la madera, la tela, el cuero, el papiro, la carne, todo ido, dejando mayormente piedra y barro cocido. Las inscripciones escritas, que más nos dicen, son las supervivencias más raras de todas. Y todo objeto que se halla debe aún interpretarse — fecharse, identificarse, encajarse en una historia — y la interpretación puede revisarse. Así que la arqueología no es una máquina en la que metes un versículo bíblico y recibes un veredicto de "verdadero" o "falso". Es una lectura paciente, parcial y humana de los restos dispersos del pasado. Entender esa limitación es el principio de usar este testigo con honestidad, pues explica de inmediato por qué la arqueología tan rara vez prueba, y por qué su silencio prueba aún menos.

blocks.en: 3. The Three Things the Spade Can Do
blocks.es_reference: 3. Las Tres Cosas que la Pala Puede Hacer

blocks.en: Recall the three things evidence can do, which we learned in the very first unit, and see how each applies to the spade. Evidence can prove — settle a matter beyond dispute — but in archaeology, as in all of history, real proof is rare; we almost never get it. Evidence can corroborate — confirm and support, line up with a claim, make it credible — and this is what archaeology does best and most often. When a dig turns up a king the Bible names, a city the Bible places just there, a custom the Bible describes, that is corroboration, the honest workhorse. And evidence can illustrate — make the real vivid before our eyes. When we uncover the very pavement where a trial was held, or a house like the ones the first Christians met in, or a lamp such as the wise virgins carried, the world of the Bible comes alive, and we read it with new sight. Corroboration and illustration are the daily work of biblical archaeology; proof is the rare exception. This is why our maxim holds: correlation, not proof. To expect proof from archaeology is to ask of it what it was never able to give — and to miss the very real gift it does give.
blocks.es_reference: Recuerda las tres cosas que la evidencia puede hacer, que aprendimos en la primera unidad, y ve cómo cada una se aplica a la pala. La evidencia puede probar — zanjar un asunto sin disputa — pero en la arqueología, como en toda la historia, la prueba real es rara; casi nunca la obtenemos. La evidencia puede corroborar — confirmar y apoyar, concordar con una afirmación, hacerla creíble — y esto es lo que la arqueología hace mejor y con más frecuencia. Cuando una excavación saca a la luz un rey que la Biblia nombra, una ciudad que la Biblia ubica justo allí, una costumbre que la Biblia describe, eso es corroboración, la herramienta honesta. Y la evidencia puede ilustrar — hacer vívido lo real ante nuestros ojos. Cuando descubrimos el mismísimo pavimento donde se celebró un juicio, o una casa como aquellas en que se reunían los primeros cristianos, o una lámpara como las que llevaban las vírgenes prudentes, el mundo de la Biblia cobra vida, y lo leemos con nueva vista. La corroboración y la ilustración son el trabajo diario de la arqueología bíblica; la prueba es la rara excepción. Por esto se mantiene nuestra máxima: correlación, no prueba. Esperar prueba de la arqueología es pedirle lo que nunca pudo dar — y perder el don muy real que sí da.

blocks.en: 4. The Skeptic's Error: Arguing from Silence
blocks.es_reference: 4. El Error del Escéptico: Argumentar desde el Silencio

blocks.en: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
blocks.es_reference: La ausencia de evidencia no es evidencia de ausencia.

blocks.en: Now the first great error, and it belongs to the skeptic. Because archaeology is so incomplete, the absence of a find can never, by itself, be a verdict. Yet again and again something in the Bible has been declared unhistorical simply because no trace of it had turned up — and then the trace turned up. For many years some scholars taught that the Hittites, a people the Old Testament mentions dozens of times, were a biblical fiction, since no independent record of them was known; today we possess vast archives of the Hittite empire, and their reality is beyond question. For a time it was said that King David was a legend, until a stone was found at Tel Dan bearing the words "the house of David." The existence of Pontius Pilate, of the Assyrian king Sargon, of the pools of Jerusalem where Jesus healed — all were doubted, and all have been confirmed by the spade. So the skeptic who reasons "no evidence has been found, therefore it did not happen" is swallowing a camel: he mistakes a gap in what the spade has reached for a proof of what never was. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. This is the first rule of the road.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora el primer gran error, y pertenece al escéptico. Porque la arqueología es tan incompleta, la ausencia de un hallazgo nunca puede, por sí sola, ser un veredicto. Sin embargo, una y otra vez algo en la Biblia ha sido declarado no histórico simplemente porque ningún rastro de ello había aparecido — y luego el rastro apareció. Por muchos años algunos eruditos enseñaron que los hititas, un pueblo que el Antiguo Testamento menciona docenas de veces, eran una ficción bíblica, ya que no se conocía ningún registro independiente de ellos; hoy poseemos vastos archivos del imperio hitita, y su realidad está fuera de duda. Por un tiempo se dijo que el rey David era una leyenda, hasta que se halló una piedra en Tel Dan que llevaba las palabras "la casa de David". La existencia de Poncio Pilato, del rey asirio Sargón, de los estanques de Jerusalén donde Jesús sanó — todos fueron dudados, y todos han sido confirmados por la pala. Así que el escéptico que razona "no se ha hallado evidencia, por tanto no sucedió" traga un camello: confunde un vacío en lo que la pala ha alcanzado con una prueba de lo que nunca fue. La ausencia de evidencia no es evidencia de ausencia. Esta es la primera regla del camino.

blocks.en: 5. The Apologist's Error: Overclaiming
blocks.es_reference: 5. El Error del Apologista: Exagerar

blocks.en: But the opposite error is just as real, and it belongs to us. The eager believer, wanting to defend the Bible, seizes on every discovery and cries, "Archaeology proves the Bible!" He means well, but he promises what archaeology cannot deliver, and in doing so he builds the very trap his brother will fall into. For archaeology does not prove the Bible; it correlates with it. And when the believer who has been told "it is all proven" meets a genuine dispute — a dig whose dating is contested, a wall whose fall is argued over, an event for which no clear evidence yet stands — his faith can be shaken far more violently than the difficulty deserved, because it had been resting on a promise that was never true. This is the gnat-strain of Matthew twenty-three: straining after more certainty than the evidence holds, and swallowing a hidden camel of future doubt. We refuse this overclaim not because we lack confidence in the Bible, but precisely to protect the faith of those we teach. An honest correlation, soberly stated, is a firmer foundation than a proof that cannot bear weight. We will say what the evidence says, and no more.
blocks.es_reference: Pero el error opuesto es igual de real, y nos pertenece a nosotros. El creyente entusiasta, queriendo defender la Biblia, se aferra a cada descubrimiento y clama: "¡La arqueología prueba la Biblia!" Tiene buena intención, pero promete lo que la arqueología no puede cumplir, y al hacerlo construye la misma trampa en que caerá su hermano. Pues la arqueología no prueba la Biblia; se correlaciona con ella. Y cuando el creyente al que se le dijo "todo está probado" halla una disputa genuina — una excavación cuya datación se discute, un muro cuya caída se debate, un evento para el cual aún no hay evidencia clara — su fe puede ser sacudida mucho más violentamente de lo que la dificultad merecía, porque había descansado en una promesa que nunca fue verdadera. Este es el colar el mosquito de Mateo veintitrés: buscar más certeza de la que la evidencia sostiene, y tragar un camello oculto de duda futura. Rechazamos esta exageración no porque nos falte confianza en la Biblia, sino precisamente para proteger la fe de aquellos a quienes enseñamos. Una correlación honesta, dicha con sobriedad, es un fundamento más firme que una prueba que no puede sostener peso. Diremos lo que la evidencia dice, y nada más.

blocks.en: 6. How Correlation Builds Honest Confidence
blocks.es_reference: 6. Cómo la Correlación Construye Confianza Honesta

blocks.en: If archaeology only correlates and never proves, someone may ask, what is it really worth? A very great deal — for the cumulative weight of honest correlation is powerful. The Bible is crowded with checkable claims: it names kings and nations and officials, it places cities and battles and building projects, it describes coins and courts and customs. And across a century and a half of excavation, these checkable details have been confirmed on an enormous scale. Time and again the Bible's world has proven to be the real world of the ancient Near East, precise in its geography, accurate in its politics, at home in its own age. Now, a document that gets its verifiable world right, over and over, in a thousand incidental details, earns a reasonable trust for the rest of its account. This is corroboration doing exactly its proper work. It does not prove that the sea parted or that the tomb was empty — no spade can reach a miracle. But it shows that the Bible is not an account detached from history; it is a record rooted in real places and real events, among real people. That is a modest claim, and it is a strong one, and it is true.
blocks.es_reference: Si la arqueología solo se correlaciona y nunca prueba, alguien preguntará: ¿qué vale en realidad? Muchísimo — pues el peso acumulado de la correlación honesta es poderoso. La Biblia está llena de afirmaciones verificables: nombra reyes y naciones y funcionarios, ubica ciudades y batallas y proyectos de construcción, describe monedas y tribunales y costumbres. Y a través de siglo y medio de excavación, estos detalles verificables han sido confirmados a una escala enorme. Una y otra vez el mundo de la Biblia ha resultado ser el mundo real del antiguo Cercano Oriente, preciso en su geografía, exacto en su política, en casa en su propia época. Ahora bien, un documento que acierta su mundo verificable, una y otra vez, en mil detalles incidentales, gana una confianza razonable para el resto de su relato. Esto es la corroboración haciendo exactamente su trabajo propio. No prueba que el mar se partió ni que la tumba estaba vacía — ninguna pala puede alcanzar un milagro. Pero muestra que la Biblia no es un relato separado de la historia; es un registro arraigado en lugares y acontecimientos reales, entre personas reales. Esa es una afirmación modesta, y es una afirmación fuerte, y es verdadera.

blocks.en: 7. Where the Witness Falls Silent
blocks.es_reference: 7. Dónde el Testigo Enmudece

blocks.en: No spade can reach a miracle.
blocks.es_reference: Ninguna pala puede alcanzar un milagro.

blocks.en: We must be equally clear about where this witness falls silent, for its limits are as important as its strength. Archaeology can confirm that a city was destroyed by fire; it cannot tell you that the LORD gave it into Israel's hand. It can show that a man named Jesus was crucified in Judea under Pontius Pilate; it cannot show that on the third day He rose. It reaches the material and the datable — walls, bones, coins, names — and there it stops. It cannot reach the miracle, or the meaning, or the God who stands behind the event. And this is not a weakness we must hide; it is simply the shape of the tool. The deepest truths of the faith were never meant to be dug out of the ground. They rest, as we said at the very beginning, on the character of the God who spoke and the witness of His Spirit. So archaeology takes its proper place: not the foundation of our faith, but a supporting witness to the world in which our faith's events occurred. It corroborates the stage and the actors; it cannot script the drama, and it does not need to.
blocks.es_reference: Debemos ser igual de claros sobre dónde este testigo enmudece, pues sus límites son tan importantes como su fuerza. La arqueología puede confirmar que una ciudad fue destruida por fuego; no puede decirte que Jehová la entregó en mano de Israel. Puede mostrar que un hombre llamado Jesús fue crucificado en Judea bajo Poncio Pilato; no puede mostrar que al tercer día resucitó. Alcanza lo material y lo datable — muros, huesos, monedas, nombres — y ahí se detiene. No puede alcanzar el milagro, ni el significado, ni el Dios que está detrás del evento. Y esto no es una debilidad que debamos ocultar; es sencillamente la forma de la herramienta. Las verdades más profundas de la fe nunca fueron destinadas a ser desenterradas de la tierra. Descansan, como dijimos al mismísimo principio, en el carácter del Dios que habló y el testimonio de su Espíritu. Así que la arqueología toma su lugar propio: no el fundamento de nuestra fe, sino un testigo que apoya el mundo en que ocurrieron los eventos de nuestra fe. Corrobora el escenario y los actores; no puede escribir el drama, y no necesita hacerlo.

blocks.en: 8. The Rules for the Road Ahead
blocks.es_reference: 8. Las Reglas para el Camino que Sigue

blocks.en: So we have the rules by which to hear this third witness, and they are worth gathering in one place. Expect correlation, not proof. Never argue from silence, in either direction, for the ground is only partly dug. Refuse the skeptic's camel, that a missing find is a verdict; and refuse the apologist's overclaim, that a lucky find proves all things. Where a genuine dispute stands — and there are a few — hold it honestly as an open question, remembering that both the reading of the Bible and the reading of the dig can be revisited as more is learned. Let the great cumulative weight of real correlations build an honest and unhurried confidence. And remember always that this witness testifies to the world of the Bible, never to its miracles or its meaning. With these rules in hand, we are ready to walk among the actual finds — the confirmations that answered the skeptics and the honest puzzles that remain unsettled. In the next unit, the spade itself will testify: the stones that speak for Scripture, and the questions we are still content to leave open.
blocks.es_reference: Así que tenemos las reglas para oír a este tercer testigo, y vale reunirlas en un solo lugar. Espera correlación, no prueba. Nunca argumentes desde el silencio, en ninguna dirección, pues la tierra está solo parcialmente excavada. Rechaza el camello del escéptico, de que un hallazgo faltante es un veredicto; y rechaza la exageración del apologista, de que un hallazgo afortunado prueba todas las cosas. Donde hay una disputa genuina — y hay unas pocas — sostenla con honestidad como una pregunta abierta, recordando que tanto la lectura de la Biblia como la lectura de la excavación pueden revisarse conforme se aprende más. Deja que el gran peso acumulado de correlaciones reales construya una confianza honesta y sin prisa. Y recuerda siempre que este testigo testifica del mundo de la Biblia, nunca de sus milagros ni de su significado. Con estas reglas en mano, estamos listos para caminar entre los hallazgos reales — las confirmaciones que respondieron a los escépticos y los enigmas honestos que quedan sin resolver. En la próxima unidad, la pala misma testificará: las piedras que hablan por la Escritura, y las preguntas que aún estamos contentos de dejar abiertas.

Confusing correlation with proof, in either direction, leads a believer to stumble.

sa.prompt: Explain why archaeology so rarely proves and why its silence proves even less.
sa.model: Archaeology is a science of fragments: only a fraction of ancient sites are found, only a fraction excavated, and most materials perish, while inscriptions are rarest of all, and every find must still be interpreted. Because so little survives and is recovered, a matter is rarely settled beyond dispute, and the mere absence of a find proves even less, since the ground is only partly dug.

sa.prompt: Name and apply the three things evidence can do to archaeology.
sa.model: Proof settles a matter beyond dispute, and in archaeology it is rare. Corroboration confirms and supports — a king, city, or custom the Bible names turning up in the ground — and this is what archaeology does best. Illustration makes the world of the text vivid, as when a lamp or a house or a pavement from Bible times is uncovered. Corroboration and illustration are the daily work of biblical archaeology.

sa.prompt: Explain "absence of evidence is not evidence of absence," with an example.
sa.model: Because archaeology is so incomplete, a missing find can never by itself be a verdict. Again and again the Bible has been called unhistorical because nothing had turned up, and then it did. The Hittites were once dismissed as a fiction until vast archives were found; King David was called a legend until a stone at Tel Dan named "the house of David." So the skeptic who says "no evidence, therefore it did not happen" swallows a camel.

sa.prompt: Why does the unit refuse the overclaim "Archaeology proves the Bible"?
sa.model: Because archaeology does not prove the Bible; it correlates with it. The believer told "it is all proven," when he later meets a genuine dispute, can have his faith shaken far more than the difficulty deserved, since it rested on a promise that was never true. The unit refuses the overclaim not from weakness but to protect the faith of those we teach; honest correlation is a firmer foundation than a proof that cannot bear weight.

sa.prompt: If archaeology only correlates, what is it worth?
sa.model: A great deal, because the cumulative weight of honest correlation is powerful. The Bible names many checkable kings, nations, cities, and customs, and across a century and a half of excavation these details have been confirmed on an enormous scale. A document that gets its verifiable world right again and again earns reasonable trust for the rest of its account — not proof of the miracles, but strong evidence that the Bible is rooted in real history, not detached from it.

Archaeology reaches the material and the datable — walls, bones, coins, names — and there it stops. It can confirm that a city burned but not that the LORD gave it to Israel; it can show that Jesus was crucified under Pilate but not that He rose on the third day. It cannot reach the miracle, the meaning, or the God behind the event. The deepest truths of the faith were never meant to be dug out of the ground.

sa.prompt: What are the rules for weighing archaeological evidence, according to the unit?
sa.model: Expect correlation, not proof. Never argue from silence in either direction, since the ground is only partly dug. Refuse the skeptic's camel that a missing find is a verdict, and refuse the apologist's overclaim that a find proves all things. Hold genuine disputes honestly as open questions, and let the cumulative weight of real correlations build an unhurried confidence, remembering that archaeology reaches the world of the Bible but not its miracles.

sa.prompt: Explain archaeology's proper place in relation to faith.
sa.model: Archaeology is not the foundation of faith but a supporting witness to the world in which faith's events occurred. It corroborates the stage and the actors — real places, real people, real history — but it cannot script the drama or reach the miracle. Our faith rests, as from the beginning, on the character of the God who spoke and the witness of His Spirit, and archaeology takes its modest, honest place beside that foundation, not in place of it.

sa.prompt: In your own words, how should the rules of this unit guide you when you hear a claim about archaeology and the Bible?
sa.model: When I hear that a find "proves the Bible," I should remember it correlates rather than proves, and state it soberly. When I hear that a missing find shows the Bible is false, I should recall that absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. I should refuse both extremes, hold genuine disputes as open questions, and rest my faith not on the spade but on God, letting real correlations build honest confidence.
